About Me

I'm Riddhima Kapoor, a Fashion Technology student at NIFT (BFT), with my foundation built in production merchandising. From there, my interest has moved toward the retail side of fashion — the business of it, where consumer behaviour and point-of-sale signal actually shape what gets bought and sold.

Along the way, I've picked up a habit of building things: tools and models that take scattered data and turn it into something people can actually act on.

That's the instinct I want to carry into retail merchandising and buying, where data meets the decisions that drive a brand forward.

Project from CTA Apparels

Even in 2026, most merchandising teams still don't have systems that actually support their decision-making. Why are we still manually filling spreadsheets and opening 15 different files just to understand order status?

The data exists — it's even semi-consolidated — but it's not built to be worked with.
So I built something that is.

Excel Prototype Shipment Risk Signal My Next Step T&A Monitoring System
in short.txt

In Short

Existing ERP Context:

  • CTA's ERP (Task Manager) shows live status — where every style stands today — but has no T&A calendars built in at all, no forward-looking target dates, and no plan-vs-actual comparison
  • So shipment risk stayed invisible until a milestone was already missed, with no way to rank which delays actually mattered
  • This project adds that missing layer: a single risk-scored, ranked view that flags which styles need attention before the shipment buffer erodes — not after

What the dashboard offers:

  • Auto-generates T&A calendars per style, per merchandiser — something the ERP has no equivalent for
  • Minimal manual input — only the Actual Date needs to be entered once a milestone completes; everything else (status, delay days, risk score, category) is a formula
  • Easy-to-view, decision-ready layout — KPI cards, a ranked worklist (Top 10 highest-risk styles), and colour-coded Green/Yellow/Red flags so a merchandiser can scan and act in under a minute

This fixes a major obvious gap in the industry. We have all the data in the world, we just need to use it better.

Opening 15 different excel sheets sitting individually on your laptop vs One simple solution.

risk parameters.xlsx

Project Framework

raw data → derived metrics → aggregated summary → visual layer → decision.

  1. → T&A Plans(Per style, per merchandiser)
  2. → Data Consolidation(Style_Master + Generated_TA)
  3. → Risk Scoring Engine(Weighted delay + buffer penalty, One row per style: score, category)
  4. → Dashboard(KPIs, Top-10, hotspots)
  5. → Merchandiser Action(Follow-up & escalation)
integration + future scope

Integration with existing ERP:

  • Built as a standalone Excel prototype for this phase
  • Designed to eventually fold into CTA's existing ERP rather than replace it — sitting inside the Task Manager merchandisers already use daily

Future scope — AI/ML:

  • Current model is rule-based and fully explainable by design (a manager can see exactly why a style scored what it did)
  • Next step: use historical order and delay data to move toward predictive delay forecasting
  • Goal: flag which styles are likely to slip — by buyer, process stage, or season — before the current milestone even shows signs of trouble, with today's rule-based score as the auditable baseline

research paper from nift coursework

Research Paper from NIFT Coursework

The Absence of a Standardized Framework for Measuring Sustainable Fashion Consumption: A Critical Review and Conceptual Proposal

The Problem:

Consumption — what people buy and why — drives most of a garment's lifetime environmental impact, yet it's the stage measurement handles worst. Industry tools (LCA, Higg Index) rigorously score products and factories but stop at the point of sale, and even Higg has been shown to misrank materials (polyester scoring "greener" than cotton) depending on weighting choices. Academic research fills the consumer gap but leans on self-reported surveys that poorly predict behavior (only ~30% of "ethical" intenders follow through when observed), leaving the field split and contradicting itself on basic questions like willingness to pay a sustainability premium.

The gap this creates:

  • Studies contradict each other on basic questions (do consumers pay more for sustainability? how big is the attitude-behaviour gap?) because everyone's measuring something different
iscm framework

The proposed fix — ISCM, a 5-dimension framework:

  1. Environmental Perception
  2. Social & Ethical Perception
  3. Cognitive Alignment (the novel piece — measures the gap between what people say and do, not just the attitude or the behaviour alone)
  4. Economic Feasibility
  5. Behavioural Engagement (the actual outcome — acquisition, usage, reuse, disposal)

Why it matters for Merchandising / Industry work:

  • This is the same instinct behind my CTA Apparels dashboard — building a structured, comparable system where none existed, instead of relying on scattered, self-reported, or inconsistent inputs
customer segmentation.R

Segmenting Apparel Customers to Drive Merchandising Strategy

The business gap: Retailers collect purchase data on every customer but usually act on it in bulk — same email, same discount, same seasonal push, regardless of who the customer actually is. That's expensive and leaves money on the table: premium customers get discounted unnecessarily, price-sensitive customers get ignored until they churn.

Premium CustomersHigh Spending
Low Value CustomersLow Spending, Low frequency
Frequent Buyers (Potential)High Frequency

Dataset Overview

  • Variables used:
    • Purchase Frequency per Month
    • Avg Purchase Value (INR)
  • Each row represents a customer

head(df)

why clustering

Why clustering, specifically

You don't start with predefined customer "types" — you let the purchase data (frequency + spend) reveal natural groupings first, rather than assuming segments upfront. That's the justification for K-Means over just eyeballing the data or using arbitrary spend thresholds.

data processing.R

Data Processing

  • Selected relevant features
  • Applied scaling (normalization)
  • Required for distance-based algorithms

K-Means Clustering

  • Used to create customer segments
  • Applied with K = 3 clusters
  • Groups customers based on similarity
cluster scatter plot

Cluster Scatter Plot

  • 1 (Red) — Premium Customers: high spending
  • 2 (Green) — Low-Value Customers: low spending & low frequency
  • 3 (Blue) — Frequent Buyers / Potential: high frequency
why knn

Why add KNN on top

Segmentation is only useful if it scales. K-Means gives you groups for customers you already have; KNN is what lets you slot every new customer into the right segment automatically, in real time, without re-running clustering each time.

That's the justification for combining unsupervised + supervised — one defines the strategy, the other operationalizes it. Small sample size — accuracy here is directional (proof of method), not a production-scale benchmark.

model evaluation.R

Model Evaluation

  • Data split: 70% train / 30% test
  • KNN applied with K = 5
  • Performance evaluated using:
    • Confusion matrix
    • Accuracy
0.9666667Accuracy
use & marketing strategy

Use & marketing strategy

This segmentation replaces one blanket campaign with three targeted ones, matched to each group's price sensitivity and loyalty. Channel and category data (e.g., Premium skewing Omnichannel) can sharpen this further, turning one generic campaign into three margin-aware ones.

premium

Premium gets no-discount personalization

Early access, exclusives, since discounting them wastes margin.

frequent / potential

Frequent/Potential gets bundle offers and loyalty thresholds

To nudge them toward Premium rather than discounts.

low-value

Low-Value gets seasonal promos and discount-led reactivation

Where price sensitivity is highest.

how i work

How I Work

raw data → derived metrics → aggregated summary → visual layer → decision.

How I work:

  • Find the actual bottleneck first — with CTA, it wasn't "no data," it was 15 disconnected files with no forward-looking view
  • Prototype fast and cheap (Excel, R) before reaching for anything heavier — a rule-based, explainable model beats a black-box one until the simple version stops being enough
  • Build for the person who'll use it daily — a merchandiser scanning a worklist in under a minute, not a dashboard that looks impressive in a review

Tools I use:

  • Excel / VBA — for rapid prototyping, formula-driven systems, T&A and risk-scoring logic
  • R (K-Means, KNN, ggplot2) — for segmentation, classification, and validating patterns in customer/behavioural data
  • ERP & Task Manager systems — understanding how tools need to sit inside existing workflows, not replace them

what's next

What's Next

I've seen how a product gets made. Now I want to own how it sells.

Working inside an export house taught me where product comes from — sourcing, T&A, buyer timelines, the operational reality behind every SKU. What I don't yet have full visibility into is what happens after: how that product performs at the point of sale, and why a consumer picks it up or walks past it.

My Graduation Project will focus on Retail Merchandising and Consumer Behaviour Analytics — building a structured way to connect POS-level signal (what's actually selling, to whom, how fast) with the buying and assortment decisions merchandisers make upstream. The instinct is the same one behind the CTA dashboard and my ISCM research: don't rely on scattered or self-reported inputs when a structured, comparable system can replace them.
